questions.question: In the context of language models, what is meant by a scaling law?
questions.choice_A: An empirical power-law relationship linking model size, dataset size, and compute to performance metrics like loss or perplexity
questions.choice_B: A formal proof that larger models always outperform smaller ones
questions.choice_C: A scheduling policy for increasing the learning rate with batch size
questions.choice_D: A regulatory rule about the maximum number of parameters allowed in deployed models

questions.question: Kaplan et al. (2020) reported that test loss decreases approximately as a power law with respect to model size and dataset size. Which statement best captures the practical implication?
questions.choice_A: Doubling parameters guarantees halving the loss
questions.choice_B: Returns diminish as you scale; to maintain efficiency you should co-scale parameters, data, and compute
questions.choice_C: Performance is insensitive to dataset size once a model reaches a billion parameters
questions.choice_D: Compute has no measurable impact compared to parameters and data

questions.question: What key revision did the Chinchilla results introduce relative to Kaplan’s original guidance?
questions.choice_A: They showed that loss scales linearly—not as a power law—with parameters
questions.choice_B: They recommended always maximizing parameter count and minimizing training tokens
questions.choice_C: They found models were typically under-trained on data and that, for compute-optimality, one should use more training tokens with smaller models
questions.choice_D: They concluded scaling laws do not hold beyond 1B parameters

questions.question: Which statement describes the compute-optimal allocation between parameters (N) and training tokens (T) under Chinchilla-style scaling?
questions.choice_A: T should be held constant while N increases
questions.choice_B: N should be held constant while T increases
questions.choice_C: T should grow sublinearly with N (e.g., $T \propto N^{1/2}$)
questions.choice_D: T should grow approximately linearly with N (i.e., $T \propto N$), keeping parameter and data scaling balanced

questions.question: How would you characterize an “undertrained” model in the scaling-law sense?
questions.choice_A: It has too few training tokens relative to its parameter count, so it sits above the compute-optimal loss curve
questions.choice_B: It uses too small a batch size for its learning rate schedule
questions.choice_C: It has been trained past the point of zero training loss
questions.choice_D: It uses mixed precision during training

questions.question: You have a fixed compute budget. According to Chinchilla-style guidance, which lever most reliably improves test loss?
questions.choice_A: Increasing the context window without changing anything else
questions.choice_B: Allocating more training tokens and slightly fewer parameters to match the compute-optimal ratio
questions.choice_C: Switching to a deeper but narrower network at the same parameter count
questions.choice_D: Increasing dropout during training

questions.question: Which of the following is a common pitfall when empirically evaluating scaling laws?
questions.choice_A: Using log-log plots to visualize loss versus parameters
questions.choice_B: Measuring perplexity instead of cross-entropy
questions.choice_C: Benchmark contamination, distribution shift, or data deduplication issues that falsely improve measured scaling
questions.choice_D: Training on a mixture of domains

questions.question: What does it mean to compare models at “isoFLOPs” (or isocompute) when interpreting scaling results?
questions.choice_A: Both models use the same number of parameters
questions.choice_B: Both models have identical wall-clock training time
questions.choice_C: Both models are trained on the same number of tokens
questions.choice_D: Both models are trained with equal total floating-point operations, allowing fair comparison across precision or architecture

questions.question: How are cross-entropy loss and perplexity related in language modeling?
questions.choice_A: Perplexity is the exponential of the cross-entropy in nats, $\text{PPL} = e^{L}$
questions.choice_B: Perplexity equals cross-entropy multiplied by sequence length
questions.choice_C: Cross-entropy is the inverse of perplexity
questions.choice_D: There is no simple relationship

questions.question: When fitting a power-law scaling model (e.g., $L = a N^{-\alpha}$), what is a practical indicator that the power law no longer holds in a given regime?
questions.choice_A: The learning rate schedule has multiple warmup phases
questions.choice_B: Systematic curvature appears in the log-log loss vs. size plot, indicating a break from linearity
questions.choice_C: Validation loss fluctuates within one standard deviation
questions.choice_D: The model reaches zero training loss

questions.question: How does data quality influence observed scaling exponents and constants?
questions.choice_A: It does not; only quantity matters for scaling exponents
questions.choice_B: Higher-quality data worsens scaling constants but improves exponents
questions.choice_C: Better-quality data can shift the loss curve downward (better constants) and sometimes alter the apparent exponent by changing the effective difficulty
questions.choice_D: Data quality only affects overfitting, not scaling trends

questions.question: What is the meaning of the “compute-optimal frontier” in scaling analyses?
questions.choice_A: The largest model that can fit in GPU memory
questions.choice_B: The smallest batch size that yields stable optimization
questions.choice_C: The set of configurations with identical parameter counts but different training durations
questions.choice_D: The curve giving the best achievable loss for a given total training compute by appropriately trading off parameters and tokens

questions.question: Why do practitioners often adjust batch size and learning rate together when scaling up training?
questions.choice_A: To preserve optimization dynamics (e.g., noise scale) so that the training trajectory remains comparable across scales
questions.choice_B: To keep the number of parameters constant
questions.choice_C: To align with the theoretical requirement that learning rate must be inversely proportional to model depth
questions.choice_D: Because larger batches always improve generalization

questions.question: How can architectural changes (e.g., adding optimized attention variants) complicate the interpretation of scaling laws?
questions.choice_A: They remove the need for any compute budget planning
questions.choice_B: They change constants and sometimes effective exponents, so iso-parameter comparisons can be misleading without isoFLOPs normalization
questions.choice_C: They make loss independent of token count
questions.choice_D: They ensure that extrapolations never fail

questions.question: Which statement best describes parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) in the context of scaling laws?
questions.choice_A: PEFT increases the pretraining compute-optimal token count
questions.choice_B: PEFT raises pretraining perplexity but improves downstream evaluation
questions.choice_C: PEFT leverages a large pretrained model’s representational capacity with minimal additional parameters, so pretraining scaling still dominates overall capabilities
questions.choice_D: PEFT replaces the need for large-scale pretraining entirely

questions.question: How might pruning or quantization affect empirical scaling evaluations?
questions.choice_A: They always improve the observed exponent
questions.choice_B: They leave loss unchanged if applied after training
questions.choice_C: They only influence latency, not accuracy
questions.choice_D: They can shift constants (and sometimes degrade loss), so comparisons should be made at isoFLOPs or with careful calibration

questions.question: What is the difference between iso-parameter and iso-compute comparisons when evaluating scaling claims?
questions.choice_A: Iso-parameter holds N fixed; iso-compute holds total training FLOPs fixed, which is more appropriate when precision and throughput differ
questions.choice_B: They are equivalent in practice
questions.choice_C: Iso-parameter is always preferable because parameters determine capacity
questions.choice_D: Iso-compute comparisons ignore training tokens

questions.question: How does tokenization design impact scaling-law interpretation?
questions.choice_A: It has no effect as long as the vocabulary size exceeds 32k
questions.choice_B: Different tokenizations change the number of tokens per document and the distribution of subwords, affecting both the token count and the effective difficulty of prediction
questions.choice_C: It only affects inference speed, not loss
questions.choice_D: It forces the exponent to be exactly 0.076 across datasets

questions.question: You want to empirically verify the optimal ratio between parameters and tokens under a fixed compute budget. Which experimental design is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: Train a single model size across many seeds
questions.choice_B: Vary the learning rate while keeping parameters and tokens fixed
questions.choice_C: Sweep along rays of constant total FLOPs, varying N and T jointly, and measure the loss to find the minimum on that iso-compute slice
questions.choice_D: Hold tokens fixed and maximize parameters

questions.question: Which limitation most commonly undermines naive extrapolation of scaling laws to larger regimes?
questions.choice_A: The need to use LayerNorm
questions.choice_B: The impossibility of measuring validation loss accurately
questions.choice_C: The requirement to use GELU activations
questions.choice_D: Regime changes such as data quality shifts, optimization instabilities, or architectural bottlenecks that break the previously fit power law
